title: Understanding the Menstrual Cycle
content:
The menstrual cycle is the monthly hormonal process the body goes through to prepare for a possible pregnancy. By convention, a cycle is counted from the first day of one period to the first day of the next. While a 28-day cycle is often used as a textbook example, healthy cycles commonly range from about 21 to 35 days in adults, and irregularity is common in the first few years after periods start and again in the years leading up to menopause.

The cycle is generally described in phases. During the menstrual phase, if a pregnancy has not occurred, the lining of the uterus (the endometrium) is shed, and this blood and tissue leave the body through the vagina. A period typically lasts three to seven days, though this varies by individual.

After bleeding ends, the body enters the follicular phase. Rising estrogen causes the uterine lining to thicken again, while several follicles in the ovary begin to mature. One follicle typically becomes dominant. Around the middle of an average cycle, a surge in luteinizing hormone (LH) triggers ovulation: the release of a mature egg from the dominant follicle. In a 28-day cycle this often occurs around day 12–14, but the exact timing varies significantly between individuals and even cycle to cycle in the same person.

After ovulation, the ruptured follicle transforms into a structure called the corpus luteum, which produces progesterone. Progesterone helps prepare the uterine lining to support a fertilized egg if implantation occurs. If pregnancy does not occur, progesterone and estrogen levels fall, the corpus luteum breaks down, and the uterine lining sheds — starting the next period and beginning the cycle again.

Hormonal shifts across the cycle can produce a range of normal physical and emotional changes: mild bloating, breast tenderness, mood changes, and changes in energy or appetite are common, particularly in the days before a period (sometimes described as premenstrual symptoms). These are usually not a cause for concern on their own.

What counts as "normal" varies a great deal between individuals. Useful things to track include cycle length (day 1 of one period to day 1 of the next), how many days bleeding lasts, how heavy the flow is, and any symptoms that come with it. Consistently tracking these details over a few cycles can make it much easier to notice a genuine change later and to have a more productive conversation with a clinician if something feels off.

Some degree of cycle-to-cycle variation is expected and not automatically a sign of a problem. However, patterns worth discussing with a clinician include cycles that are consistently shorter than about 21 days or longer than about 35 days, periods that stop for more than three months without pregnancy or breastfeeding as an explanation, bleeding that is unusually heavy or prolonged, or a noticeable, sustained change from a person's own typical pattern. This general information is not a diagnosis — a clinician can consider it alongside a full history, examination, and any relevant testing.
